title: Incident Types and Playbooks
learning_outcomes: Explain the purpose and key terminology of Incident Types and Playbooks.
Apply incident types and playbooks to a small synthetic example and identify evidence that supports the conclusion.
Identify a relevant limitation or failure mode and describe a safe defensive response.

content.intro: This lesson covers incident types and playbooks in the Incident Response and Recovery track. It preserves the PDF's listed subtopics and develops a small, checkable defensive example. You will practice stating scope and assumptions, selecting relevant evidence, and describing what remains uncertain.
content.why_it_matters: Follow the current organization-specific plan and NIST SP 800-61 Rev. 3; do not improvise disruptive actions when escalation is required. The specific focus here is incident types and playbooks; connect each subtopic to an observable check or a documented decision.

content_blocks.title: Core idea
content_blocks.text: Incident Types and Playbooks focuses on phishing and account compromise; ransomware and destructive malware; data breach and information disclosure. Define the system or data in scope, the expected behavior, and the consequences if that behavior fails. Then select a proportionate control and identify evidence that can verify both the normal path and an important failure case.

items.title: Phishing and Account Compromise
items.text: Social engineering manipulates trust and process. Encourage independent verification through a known channel, easy reporting, least-privileged workflows, and non-punitive incident disclosure rather than relying only on awareness slogans.

items.title: Ransomware and Destructive Malware
items.text: Malware analysis in this course is defensive: understand observable behaviors, likely impact, containment options, and safe evidence handling. Never run unknown samples on a personal or production system; use a specifically isolated lab and approved artifacts.

items.title: Data Breach and Information Disclosure
items.text: Privacy engineering limits collection and use to a defined purpose, restricts access, controls retention and deletion, and prepares for rights requests and incidents. Jurisdictional obligations require an applicability check against current official materials.

items.title: Cloud Account Compromise
items.text: Cloud and delivery security combine least-privilege identities, hardened defaults, approved dependencies, secret management, artifact provenance, logging, and repeatable deployment checks. Verify service-specific behavior and avoid placing secrets in source or logs.

items.title: Web Application Incident
items.text: For web application incident, define the expected behavior, the system or data affected, and the relevant trust boundary. Record a safe verification step and one limitation rather than treating a successful demonstration as proof of complete security.

items.title: Insider-Related Incident
items.text: For insider-related incident, define the expected behavior, the system or data affected, and the relevant trust boundary. Record a safe verification step and one limitation rather than treating a successful demonstration as proof of complete security.

content_blocks.title: Defensive example (synthetic data)
content_blocks.code:
events = [
    {"time": "09:00", "event": "alert_reviewed"},
    {"time": "09:08", "event": "account_sessions_revoked"},
    {"time": "09:20", "event": "credential_reset_verified"},
]
for event in events:
    print(event["time"], event["event"])
content_blocks.notes: This example uses synthetic values and has no network dependency. CodeLeaf displays it as instructional text; production does not execute arbitrary learner code.

content_blocks.title: Safety and verification
content_blocks.text: Incident response coordinates decisions that limit harm while preserving evidence, communicating clearly, and restoring trusted operations. Before attempting any live security test, obtain explicit permission and verify that the target and method are within scope. When a secure isolated runner is not available, treat the code as a local/synthetic example and do not run arbitrary content on production infrastructure.

content_blocks.title: Run, verify, and reset
content_blocks.text: Review the python snippet as a local calculation. If you choose to run this example, use Python 3 and synthetic inputs in a disposable local environment; compare the displayed expected output with what you observe. If the result differs, check the copied inputs and runtime version, restore the synthetic input, and repeat. No scan, external request, or production change is needed.

content_blocks.title: Recap and next step
content_blocks.text: Recap: Incident Types and Playbooks focuses on phishing and account compromise; ransomware and destructive malware; data breach and information disclosure. Define the system or data in scope, the expected behavior, and the consequences if that behavior fails. Then select a proportionate control and identify evidence that can verify both the normal path and an important failure case. Apply this to one controlled example, record evidence, and note an important edge case. Next, continue to the next lesson or revisit the prerequisite concept if a key term is unclear.

content.task: Create a concise, reviewable artifact demonstrating Incident Types and Playbooks. Use synthetic data or a controlled local training environment only. Include the relevant syllabus subtopics (Phishing and Account Compromise; Ransomware and Destructive Malware; Data Breach and Information Disclosure), state assumptions, show what evidence would support your conclusion, identify one failure mode, and recommend a defensive next step. Do not test systems outside written authorization.
task_acceptance_criteria: Use only a synthetic dataset, a disposable local lab, or an explicitly authorized system.
Include a clear scope/assumption statement and enough sanitized evidence for another learner to follow the reasoning.
Explain one limitation, edge case, or failure mode.
Recommend a proportionate defensive control and describe how to verify it safely.
hints: Write the expected behavior and test boundary before looking at a result.
Change one assumption at a time; compare results against the original synthetic case.
Record evidence and uncertainty separately, and select a proportionate protective action.
troubleshooting: The example is illustrative and should be reviewed against current platform/version documentation before production use.
If an output differs, check the input and runtime version; do not broaden the activity to an unrelated system.
Use only fake data and remove all temporary local artifacts when the exercise is complete.

common_mistakes.problem: Treating one observation as conclusive proof.
common_mistakes.why: Security telemetry and tests cover only the cases they were designed to observe.
common_mistakes.fix: Corroborate important claims and document coverage gaps.

common_mistakes.problem: Testing a target without confirming authorization.
common_mistakes.why: A technical ability to reach a system does not grant permission to assess it.
common_mistakes.fix: Use synthetic input or a local lab; stop if the approved scope is unclear.

common_mistakes.problem: Skipping the version and context assumptions.
common_mistakes.why: Security controls and protocol details vary across implementations and deployment models.
common_mistakes.fix: Record versions, configuration, expected output, and the source used for verification.

summary: Incident Types and Playbooks is best understood within its defined scope and trust boundaries.
Use relevant evidence and test both an expected case and a meaningful failure case.
Record uncertainty and choose a proportionate, authorized defensive next step.

sources.title: The NIST Cybersecurity Framework (CSF) 2.0
sources.publisher: National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST)
sources.notes: CSF 2.0 defines outcome-oriented functions and does not prescribe one mandatory implementation. Verify the current CSF resources before publication.

sources.title: CIS Critical Security Controls v8.1
sources.notes: CIS v8.1 aligns control mappings with NIST CSF 2.0. Select safeguards according to context, risk, and operating constraints.

sources.title: NIST SP 800-61 Rev. 3: Incident Response Recommendations and Considerations for Cybersecurity Risk Management
sources.notes: Final publication dated April 2025; supersedes SP 800-61 Rev. 2. Use this edition rather than older incident-response lifecycle descriptions as the primary reference.

sources.title: MITRE ATT&CK Enterprise Matrix
sources.notes: ATT&CK catalogs tactics and techniques from observed adversary behavior; it is not a deterministic attack timeline or proof that any one intrusion follows every stage.
